The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R.1) claims fiscal responsibility but hides structural rot. While ending taxes on tips and overtime puts cash back in workers’ pockets, the $50B rural hospital allocation ignores the real problem: pharmaceutical middlemen skimming 30% off every medical dollar. The $6K senior deduction? A band-aid on Medicare’s $900B annual hemorrhage to billing fraud.

Trump’s tax cuts should stay, but this 1,100-page monstrosity embeds the same DC waste it claims to fight—like $4B in redundant farm subsidies and a 15% SBA loan default rate buried in Title VII.

Real reform requires surgical cuts to bureaucracy, not another trillion-dollar piñata for lobbyists.

H.R. 2493’s Section 330A amendments prove Congress can prioritize rural health without bureaucratic bloat—if they actually enforce accountability. The bill mandates grants target underserved populations (Sec 2(a)(4)(A)), which is critical when 43% of rural mortality rates outpace urban areas. But let’s not pretend reauthorizing existing programs fixes systemic issues: $55M/year for outreach (FY2026-2030) won’t stop facility closures or workforce shortages without structural reforms.

The @HouseCommerce hearing highlighted improved A1C/blood pressure outcomes (85% grantee success in FY2022), but real progress requires defunding urban-centric waste to redirect resources. Rural Americans deserve care parity, not perpetual grant cycles that let D.C. claim “mission accomplished” while communities bleed providers.

Rulli’s right—the bill doesn’t touch disabled Ohioans, kids, or seniors. But let’s cut through the spin: Medicaid’s collapse isn’t about funding levels—it’s about systemic theft. The $50B rural hospital slush fund? A band-aid on a bullet wound.

Ohio’s Medicaid loses $55B annually to fraud, ER abuse by non-citizens, and duplicate programs. Reimbursement hikes mean nothing if bureaucrats keep burning cash on inefficiency.

Real reform requires slashing waste, enforcing eligibility, and prioritizing Americans who paid into the system.
